questions.question: When is a random variable called discrete?
options: When it can take every real value in an interval.
When its set of possible values is finite or countably infinite
When it is not a function

questions.question: What kind of possible values does a discrete random variable take?
options: Only every value in a continuum

questions.question: What kind of support does a discrete random variable have?
What determines the distribution of a discrete random variable?
How are event probabilities computed for a discrete random variable?
Which is a discrete random variable?
options: The number of emails received in an hour
A continuous waiting time measured exactly
A temperature over a real interval only

questions.question: Is the result of rolling a die discrete?
options: No, it has uncountably many possible values
Yes, it has finitely many possible values
Yes, only if the die is unfair

questions.question: Is the number of failed components in a batch discrete?
options: Yes, only if failures are impossible

questions.question: If $X$ can take only values $\{0,1,2\}$, is $X$ discrete?
options: No, finite sets are not discrete
Yes, the possible value set is finite
Only if all probabilities are equal

questions.question: If $X$ can take values $0,1,2,\ldots$, is the possible value set countably infinite?
Why is a discrete random variable natural for counts?
options: Counts take integer values, finite or countably infinite.
Counts take every real value in an interval.

questions.question: Why does a PMF determine a discrete distribution?
options: It gives only the sample-space name
It gives the probability mass at each value.
It applies only to continuous variables.

questions.question: What distinguishes a discrete variable from a continuous variable at this level?
options: Discrete variables have no generated events
Continuous variables always have finite support.
Continuous variables are not random variables
Discrete variables have finite or countable values.

questions.question: If $X$ is the number of emails in an hour, which event probability would be computed by summing masses?
A failed-component count in a batch of $5$ can take which support?
If a die-roll variable has PMF $1/6$ at each value $1,\ldots,6$, what is $P(X\in\{1,2\})$?
Why is a countably infinite support still compatible with discreteness?
options: Discrete variables must have only finitely many values
The PMF cannot sum to one
The possible values can still be listed one by one

questions.question: What would make a random variable not discrete under this definition?
options: An uncountable interval of possible values.

questions.question: A variable records an exact arrival time in $[0,1]$. Why is it not discrete?
options: It has only two possible values.
Its values form an uncountable interval.
It is a count of arrivals

questions.question: If $X$ has support $\{0,2,4,\ldots\}$, is it discrete?
options: Yes; even nonnegative integers are countable.
No, because the support is infinite.
Only if all masses are equal
